core_themes.name: Outdated match test drives chemical use
core_themes.claim: The 1988 match test is tested against an illegal, highly flammable foam that no longer reflects modern furniture construction, forcing manufacturers to over-treat cover fabrics with flame retardants to pass it.

core_themes.name: Health and environmental harm from flame retardants
core_themes.claim: Flame retardant chemicals used to meet the current test, particularly brominated FRs on cover fabrics, are linked to a growing body of evidence on endocrine, neurological, cancer and environmental harms as they migrate into dust, humans, animals and the environment.

core_themes.name: Ambiguous scope of the regulations
core_themes.claim: The prescriptive list-based scope of the 1988 regulations creates ambiguity over which products and components are covered, undermining certainty for business and consumers.

core_themes.name: Weak traceability undermines enforcement
core_themes.claim: Current traceability requirements lack supply-chain information, which is needed to enable product recall and effective enforcement by Trading Standards.

core_themes.name: Existing regulations are effective at preventing harm
core_themes.claim: The FFRs have successfully prevented substantial numbers of deaths, injuries and fires, so any reform must preserve these existing safety benefits.

core_themes.name: Preferred option: update the regulations
core_themes.claim: Updating the regulations via a new, more realistic match test is the preferred option because it meets the policy objectives of maintaining safety, reducing flame retardant use, cutting costs and improving clarity and enforcement.

core_themes.name: Removal of the cigarette test
core_themes.claim: The cigarette test should be revoked for fabrics passing the new match test because it is redundant and its removal generates additional cost savings for industry.

core_themes.name: Rejection of alternative options
core_themes.claim: Doing nothing would forgo cost and technology benefits, and revoking the regulations in favour of weaker EU standards would unacceptably increase risk to consumer safety, so neither alternative is pursued.

core_themes.name: Cost-benefit case for the proposal
core_themes.claim: The proposal is justified by a modelled net benefit (best estimate around £124m over ten years) built on quantified costs (familiarisation, transition, traceability) and benefits (reduced FR use, removal of the cigarette test), albeit with significant uncertainty in the underlying assumptions.

core_themes.name: Consultation-driven revision of the proposal
core_themes.claim: The original 2014 proposal's estimated savings and design were revised downward and reshaped in direct response to industry consultation feedback disputing the scale of benefits and raising transition cost concerns.

core_themes.name: Flexible routes to compliance
core_themes.claim: A new set of four routes to compliance (interliner, interliner+match test, protective cover, non-protective cover plus components test), developed with stakeholders, allows businesses flexibility in how they meet the revised testing requirements.

core_themes.name: Clarifying and narrowing scope
core_themes.claim: Scope will be clarified and potentially narrowed, including testing in consultation whether baby products, second-hand furniture and other grey-area items should be excluded, to reduce unnecessary testing and FR use.

core_themes.name: Strengthened traceability record-keeping
core_themes.claim: Manufacturers and importers will be required to hold more complete product and supply-chain records for an extended ten-year period to improve enforcement and recall capability.

core_themes.name: Extended transition period to limit business cost
core_themes.claim: The transition period for compliance has been lengthened to 24 months, in response to stakeholder concerns, to minimise costs from stock scrappage and early re-testing.

core_themes.name: Unresolved protective cover test to be settled via consultation
core_themes.claim: The methodology for determining whether a cover fabric qualifies as 'protective' has not yet been finalised and will be tested and developed further through consultation.
